source.version: Published journal article: Australasian Journal of Educational Technology, 2023, 39(5), 40-58 (PDF pp. 1 and 19, journal header and recommended citation). No separate revision date is stated.
source.title_on_document: Effects of a ChatGPT-based flipped learning guiding approach on learners’ courseware project performances and perceptions

supplement.holds: No supplement or appendix is referred to in the document. The PDF contains the article and references; the project rubric and outcome statistics are in the main article.

paper_design_summary: Chemistry students in two intact university classes learned to design PowerPoint courseware in a flipped classroom; the paper calls the design quasi-experimental but explicitly says one class was randomly assigned to receive ChatGPT guidance, with the other receiving traditional flipped instruction (PDF p. 9, printed p. 48, Participants; PDF p. 15, printed p. 54, Limitations). Both classes used Tencent QQ and had the same teacher; ChatGPT supplied conversational guidance during the intervention, followed by project assessment in week 8 (PDF pp. 1, 6 and 9, Abstract, learning system and Experimental procedure). Instructors rated courseware quality, while creative thinking tendency was measured by a self-report questionnaire; AI availability during production of the scored post-test project is not stated (PDF p. 10, printed p. 49, Data collection instruments and Table 1).

studies.label: Courseware project experiment in two university classes

assignment.what_was_assigned: One intact class was randomly assigned to ChatGPT-FLGA; the other class received T-FLGA. Assignment was at class level, not individual student level. The field_rct code follows this explicit assignment statement and the ordinary coursework setting, despite the author calling the study quasi-experimental.
assignment.quote: One intact class of 42 students (18 males) was randomly assigned to be the experimental group, which adopted ChatGPT-FLCA.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 48), Experimental design / Participants; also PDF p. 1 (printed p. 40), Abstract. ChatGPT-FLCA in the quote is the spelling printed in the Participants paragraph.

arms.name: ChatGPT-FLGA (experimental group)
arms.description: An intact class received the ChatGPT-based flipped learning guiding approach through the QQ learning system, alongside flipped classroom instruction and discussion with the same teacher as the control class (PDF pp. 1, 5-6 and 9, Abstract, learning system and Participants).

arms.name: T-FLGA (control group)
arms.description: The other intact class received traditional flipped learning, with QQ discussion and the same teacher, without the ChatGPT-based guiding approach (PDF pp. 1 and 9, Abstract and Participants).

participants.exclusions: No exclusions or attrition are reported. The procedure says all students completed the pre-test and post-test; the analyzed arm counts in Tables 2 and 8 are the same as the class counts at assignment. The randomized count refers to students in randomly assigned classes, not individual randomization.
participants.who: Chemistry majors taking the compulsory Modern Educational Technology course at a public normal university; mean age 20 and no prior knowledge of designing and developing courseware.
participants.quote: A total of 81 participants (aged 20 on average) were from two classes
participants.locator: PDF p. 9 (printed p. 48), Participants and Experimental procedure, gives the total and class allocation counts; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 50), Table 2, and PDF p. 13 (printed p. 52), Table 8, give analyzed counts; PDF p. 15 (printed p. 54), Limitations, identifies chemistry majors.

ai_tool.how_used: An AI teacher connected ChatGPT to Tencent QQ through a local server. Students could address it with @AI teacher for continuing conversations, answers and personalized guidance during pre-class and in-class learning; the system also sent task reminders and encouraged critical discussion. It supplied solutions, so it was not a content-free coach (PDF pp. 5-8, printed pp. 44-47, ChatGPT-FLGA and the learning system; Figure 4 on PDF p. 7).

task.description: Design and develop multimedia courseware using Microsoft PowerPoint. Learning examples include animation of a single choice and a flying centipede. Pre-project and post-project performance were assessed, but the precise scored project prompts are not reproduced, leaving uncertain how much open-ended creative design they required (PDF p. 6, printed p. 45, learning content and Figure 2; PDF pp. 9-10, printed pp. 48-49, Experimental procedure and Data collection instruments).
task.duration: The ChatGPT-FLGA/T-FLGA intervention lasted 3 weeks after the pre-test in week 4; the post-test was in week 8. A time limit for producing either scored project is not stated (PDF p. 9, printed p. 48, Experimental procedure and Figure 7).

outcomes.name: Post-project courseware performance / quality
outcomes.measure_detail: A rubric with a maximum total score of 100 assesses instruction, science, technology, artistry and operability. Two experienced educational technology instructors scored the pre-project and post-project; each student’s project score is the average of the two expert scores. The rubric assesses teaching suitability, content errors, material optimization, reasonable matching of materials and interface friendliness, rather than explicitly scoring novelty or overall creativity. Usefulness is the closest code for this product-quality composite, with creative-task eligibility unresolved. Only the aggregate performance score is reported, not separate dimension results (PDF p. 10, printed p. 49, Data collection instruments and Table 1). ANCOVA adjusts post-project scores for pre-project performance (PDF p. 11, printed p. 50, Experimental results and Table 2).
outcomes.delay: Assessment in the later week-8 session after the 3-week intervention; elapsed days and whether AI had been removed during project production are not stated (PDF p. 9, printed p. 48, Experimental procedure).

contrasts.reported: Experimental group: N = 42, Mean = 88.80, SD = 2.73, Adjusted mean = 89.93, SE = 0.43. Control group: N = 39, Mean = 87.27, SD = 3.41, Adjusted mean = 87.13, SE = 0.45. F = 8.32*, Partial η2 = 0.09; table footnote: *p < 0.05. The accompanying prose reports p = 0.00 < 0.05, reproduced as printed. SE values are for the adjusted arm means; no SE for their contrast is given. The reported standardized effect is partial eta squared, not a standardized mean difference.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 11 (printed p. 50), Project performance and Table 2.

outcomes.name: Creative thinking tendency (self-report; ineligible as an output score)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: The Creative Thinking Tendency Scale consists of five self-report items on a 5-point agreement scale; the example item is "I like to ask some questions that others do not think of." This is a questionnaire about perceived tendencies, not a creativity rating of courseware or another produced output. Retained to distinguish the paper’s explicit creativity claim from the expert-rated project outcome; it cannot meet the output-score criterion (PDF p. 10, printed p. 49, Data collection instruments). ANCOVA controls for the pre-questionnaire rating (PDF p. 11, printed p. 50, Experimental results; PDF p. 13, printed p. 52, Analysis of creative thinking tendency).
outcomes.delay: Post-questionnaire in week 8 after the 3-week intervention; elapsed days not stated. No creative output was produced for this measure (PDF p. 9, printed p. 48, Experimental procedure).

contrasts.reported: Experimental group: N = 42, Mean = 19.19, SD = 3.00, Adjusted mean = 19.07, SE = 0.44. Control group: N = 39, Mean = 17.28, SD = 3.96, Adjusted mean = 17.40, SE = 0.46. F = 6.85*, Partial η2 = 0.08; table footnote: *p < 0.05. The accompanying prose reports p = 0.01 < 0.05. SE values are for the adjusted arm means; no SE for their contrast is given. The reported standardized effect is partial eta squared, not a standardized mean difference.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 13 (printed p. 52), Analysis of creative thinking tendency and Table 8; instrument description on PDF p. 10 (printed p. 49).

company_involvement.description: No company research involvement is reported. The author has a university affiliation, and the acknowledged funder is the Ministry of Education, China. Use of ChatGPT and QQ alone is not treated as company involvement.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 40), author affiliation; PDF p. 15 (printed p. 54), Acknowledgements.

eligibility.reason: The paper explicitly reports random assignment of an intact class to ChatGPT guidance in ordinary coursework, supporting field_rct at class level despite the author’s quasi-experimental label (PDF p. 9, printed p. 48, Participants). It reports 81 students, with 42 and 39 analyzed in the two arms, meeting the people threshold (PDF p. 9, Participants; PDF p. 11, Table 2; PDF p. 13, Table 8). The explicitly named creative-thinking measure is self-report and cannot qualify (PDF p. 10, Data collection instruments; PDF p. 13, Table 8). The separate courseware score is genuinely rated on participants’ output and measures quality/usefulness, a construct permitted by the codebook for creative design tasks. However, the scored task prompts are not supplied and the learning examples are technical animation projects; the document does not establish clearly whether the assessed task requires open-ended creative design. The rubric measures instructional/technical/artistic quality without an explicit novelty or creativity criterion (PDF p. 6, learning content and Figure 2; PDF pp. 9-10, Experimental procedure and Table 1). Core eligibility therefore remains unclear pending the scope decision on that output task. AI access during production of the post-project is also unstated, so with_ai versus after_ai cannot be assigned reliably.

one_line_finding: The ChatGPT class had higher courseware quality scores (adjusted means 89.93 versus 87.13; F = 8.32, partial η2 = 0.09; PDF p. 11, Table 2) and higher self-reported creative thinking tendency (19.07 versus 17.40; F = 6.85, partial η2 = 0.08; PDF p. 13, Table 8), with no separately scored output-creativity measure.
open_questions: Does the scored pre-/post-project require open-ended creative design, making its expert-rated quality a qualifying usefulness outcome, or does it mainly test reproduction of taught PowerPoint techniques? The actual assessment prompt is not supplied (PDF p. 6, learning content and Figure 2; PDF pp. 9-10, Experimental procedure and Table 1).

Was ChatGPT available while students produced the scored post-project in week 8, or had it been removed? Intervention-period access is stated, but test-period access is not; this determines with_ai versus after_ai (PDF pp. 6 and 9, learning system and Experimental procedure).
notes: The full markdown was read from beginning to end, including all references; no appendix is present. Locators distinguish one-based PDF pages from printed journal pages. Design, participant counts, rubric and recorded statistics were checked with PyMuPDF text extraction; Figures 2, 4 and 7 were also inspected from PDF renders held in memory. There is one substantive comparative experiment. Preparatory needs interviews in the system-development section and the post-experiment qualitative interviews are not treated as additional creative-output studies (PDF pp. 5, 9 and 13). The outcomes array retains one candidate output-quality outcome and the self-report creative-thinking outcome for explicit exclusion; self-efficacy, learning attitudes and motivation are omitted because they do not score creative output. No diversity/homogenization measure is reported. The author’s quasi-experimental label does not override the explicit class-randomization statement; there is only one class in each arm, and the reported student-level ANCOVA does not describe adjustment for class clustering (PDF pp. 9 and 11). The form has no not_stated option for AI availability or unresolved question coding, so these are null where the source cannot support a choice, rather than inferring AI withdrawal from the word post-test. The self-report outcome has question none and null AI availability because it is not produced creative work. Timing is coded delayed for the later week-8 assessment session; no interval in days is inferred. Figure 7 repeats the label Pre-test and pre-questionnaire at the end, while the accompanying prose explicitly calls the week-8 assessments post-tests/post-questionnaires (PDF p. 9); timing and outcome labels follow the prose. The printed project-performance p = 0.00 is preserved, not interpreted as an exact zero or converted to another threshold. No effect sizes or contrast standard errors were computed. No preregistration, sample-reuse, supplement, or data/code availability statement is reported in the document.
